summary: Reviews examples of limited domains, also called controlled environments, where network behaviors and semantics are specific to a restricted region of the internet. Policies, options, management and security may differ from the open internet.

eli5.summary: A school playground has its own rules different from the street. This explains networks that work that way.

questions: can internet protocols behave differently inside a controlled network
what is a controlled environment in networking
why do some internet protocols only work inside one network
what are the requirements for limited domain membership
subtitle: Why some network features only make sense inside a bounded region, and what it would take to define that region securely.

tldr.problem: More and more networks need their own policies, options, management styles and security rules, yet the Internet has no well-defined concept of a limited region. Features that cross the open Internet often fail on some paths.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys examples of limited domains (also called controlled environments), offers a taxonomy for describing them, and argues that some protocols should be standardized with a limited scope. It lists functional requirements for secure domain membership.
tldr.outcome: It proposes no protocol. It concludes that explicitly defined limited-domain protocols are reasonable if they state how the domain is defined, and that precise membership definitions and secure enrolment mechanisms are needed.

today: RFC 8799 is an Informational Independent Submission, published in July 2020. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and the RFC Editor makes no statement about its value for implementation or deployment.

sections.title: What a Limited Domain Is
sections.content:
A limited domain is a network, or a region of one, with its own requirements, behaviors and semantics. It may be local in a geographical sense (a building, a campus, a vehicle) or a defined set of users or nodes joined by a virtual network over the Internet or a physical network running in parallel with it.

The word has nothing to do with DNS domains, although the two can coincide. The RFC treats limited domain and controlled environment as meaning the same thing in practice. For example, RFC 8086 says that a controlled environment has less restrictive requirements than the general Internet. Policies, default parameters, supported options, management style and security requirements can all vary from one domain to the next.

The document is the authors' own research, produced through consultation within the IETF but not a product of IETF consensus. It is an Independent Submission and is not an Internet Standards Track specification.
sections.eli5: A limited domain is a group of computers that follow their own house rules, like the people living in one apartment building.

sections.title: Failure Modes in Today's Internet
sections.content:
The RFC says the Internet has no well-defined concept of limited domains, so some protocols and features fail on certain paths. Its examples: the Internet is not transparent to IPv6 extension headers, Path MTU Discovery has been unreliable for many years, and IP fragmentation is also unreliable.

Firewalls placed at domain boundaries that humans perceive but protocols do not know about cause arbitrary failures at the application layer. Boundaries defined by address filtering rules in routers are prone to leakage through human error. Leakage is much less likely when nodes must be explicitly configured to handle a given limited-domain protocol, for example by installing a specific protocol handler.

The authors conclude that for some protocol elements transparency is a lost cause and middleboxes are here to stay, so some application environments need features that cannot, or should not, cross the whole Internet.
sections.eli5: Some toys do not work when you carry them out of the playground, because the street has gates and guards that do not know about them.

sections.title: Examples of Domains and Solutions
sections.content:
Section 3 lists 14 kinds of network with limited-domain needs, loosely from smaller to bigger: home and small office networks, vehicle networks, SCADA and other hard real-time networks, sensor and Internet-of-Things networks, constrained and delay-tolerant networks, enterprise and campus networks, service-provider VPNs, data centers, content delivery networks and massive web service provider networks. Virtual private networks, intent-based networking and network slicing also depend on the idea of a domain.

Section 4 lists 14 technical solutions that only work within a domain. They include Differentiated Services (RFC 2474), where the 6-bit Differentiated Services Code Point has locally significant values re-marked at domain boundaries, Integrated Services with RSVP, Service Function Chaining (RFC 7665) with its Network Service Header (RFC 8300), Segment Routing (RFC 8402), Deterministic Networking, Provisioning Domains, and creative uses of IPv6 such as new extension headers. Address scopes, such as link-local and Unique Local Addresses, are also mentioned for completeness.

The RFC warns that limited use is no excuse for bad design or poor security. Protocols meant for limited use are likely to be used, or misused, elsewhere, and limited use can add complexity to a protocol and its security design.
sections.eli5: There are many kinds of networks, from a home to a huge data center. Many have special tools that are only meant to be used inside their own walls.

sections.title: The Scope of Protocols in Limited Domains
sections.content:
If protocols are to be standardized for use only inside a limited domain, what happens when several domains use the same one? The RFC describes four scenarios, A to D, depending on whether the protocol respects standard IP formats, whether it is valid outside its domain, and whether the meaning of its values is the same in every domain.

Differentiated Services shows the point. A packet with any value in the 6 DSCP bits is well formed, so it fits scenario A, but the meaning of the values is locally significant, so it also fits scenario D. DSCP values are interoperable across domain boundaries only if operators agree, or if a gateway function is used.

The conclusion is that it is reasonable to define limited-domain protocols, as standards or as proprietary mechanisms, as long as they say which scenario applies and clarify how the domain is defined. If all relevant standards are respected outside the boundary, a well-specified limited-domain protocol need not damage the rest of the Internet. This is not a recommendation to abandon the goal that a standardized protocol should be global in scope.
sections.eli5: Some game rules work in any playground. Others only work in your own, and if two playgrounds join, their rules might clash. The RFC says to write down which kind your rule is.

sections.title: Functional Requirements for Domains
sections.content:
Today limited domains are created by careful configuration of boundary routers and firewalls, an error-prone method. The RFC assumes domains should be created and managed automatically, with minimal human configuration, and that membership operations should be cryptographically secured.

What matters is whether a node is a member of the domain and whether it sits at the boundary, facing both inwards and outwards. A sending node needs to know whether a destination is inside or outside, and a boundary node needs to know which interfaces face which way. The listed requirements are:

  • Domain Identity: a unique, verifiable identifier, effectively a public key whose private key holder is the trust anchor.
  • Nesting and Overlapping of domains.
  • Node Eligibility, Secure Enrollment, Withdrawal and optional Dynamic Membership.
  • Role, at simplest interior node or boundary node, plus Peer Verification and Role Verification.
  • Domain Data: policy or configuration, such as filtering policy.

Whether individual packets should carry a domain indicator, or be cryptographically authenticated, is left for further study. The RFC does not propose a design for these mechanisms.
sections.eli5: To keep the playground fair, each kid needs a membership badge, a job like gatekeeper or player, and a way to check other kids' badges.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The boundary of a limited domain often acts as a security boundary: a trust boundary and a boundary of authority for defining capabilities. Segment routing, for example, explicitly uses the concept of a trusted domain. Limited-domain features are useful inside but often meaningless or harmful if they enter or leave the domain.

The boundary also protects the confidentiality of operational parameters the operator does not want to reveal, which is separate from privacy for individual users. The security model must allow for a trust model that changes at the boundary, and credentials will typically need to be signed by a domain-specific authority. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The playground fence keeps private games private. But the fence only helps if the gate guard knows who belongs inside.

cells: Respects standard IP formats and is not blocked by firewalls
Can run between two parts of a domain over the Internet; an inter-domain protocol
Does not respect standard IP formats (for example a non-standard IPv6 extension header)
Cannot run between domains directly over IP; an intra-domain protocol
Specified to be invalid outside its domain of origin
Needs a single virtual domain, such as a tunnel; boundary nodes must drop its packets
Not interoperable in the normal sense; merging domains might fail unpredictably
